extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of mathematical analysis and foundations (advanced undergraduates, graduate students, and mathematically literate general readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and criteria for representing numbers (rationals, irrationals, transcendentals) using infinite sequences/series, and for characterizing convergence, equality, order, arithmetic, and continuity of the real-number domain (Cantor continuum).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric-series convergence criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: When we restrict ourselves to positive geometrical series, we see that the series is convergent when the ratio is less than 1, divergent otherwise. This result can be immediately generalized to alternating geometrical series (ratio negative): the alternating geometrical series will converge if the ratio is a proper fraction, diverge otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 990, 9.9, 0.099, ... is a geometric progression whose sum by the summation formula is finite (1000). Use the summation formula for geometric series; check ratio magnitude (<1) for convergence. For alternating geometric series check absolute value of ratio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodic decimal <-> rational equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Any rational number can be represented in a unique way as an infinite periodic decimal fraction; conversely, any periodic decimal fraction represents a rational number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 0.(36) = 36/99 = 4/11; mixed periodic like 0.34(53) can be converted by multiplying and algebraic manipulation (e.g., multiply by power of 10 to isolate period). Treat terminating fractions as period-zero periodic fractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-periodic decimal sequences need formal convergence definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Infinite non-periodic decimal sequences, whose digit distribution is non-repeating, are not automatically classifiable as numbers by naive intuition; the manner in which convergence and limit are defined may preclude calling such sequences numbers unless they satisfy a formal convergence criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of chaotic or non-periodic decimals (e.g., concatenation of integers). Intuitive views of 'growing yet bounded' are insufficient — require formal definition of convergence/limit to admit as numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-asymptotic property as generalized convergence (Cantor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cantor identified a property — the self-asymptotic nature of a convergent sequence — and extended convergence by identifying self-asymptotic sequences with convergent ones (hence generating real numbers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: 'advance' a sequence by deleting initial terms to produce shifted sequences; if all such shifted sequences are asymptotic (differences evanescent) the sequence is self-asymptotic. This property holds for sequences with rational limits and many non-periodic decimal sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality and order via difference-sequence behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two sequences defining real numbers a and b, form the difference sequence (A−B). If this difference sequence is evanescent, then a=b. If eventually all terms of the difference are positive, then a>b; if eventually all terms are negative, then a<b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces to the usual order when the sequences have rational limits. Use eventual sign-stability or vanishing of differences to compare real numbers defined by sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum and product defined termwise and require convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: The sum and the product of two real numbers are defined as the real numbers given by sequences obtained by adding or multiplying the corresponding terms of the defining sequences; this presupposes the resultant sequences are themselves convergent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One must prove the resulting sequences converge; then verify algebraic properties (associative, commutative, distributive) for these operations on real numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evanescence (terms -> 0) is necessary but not sufficient for series convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: The evanescence of the general term (the generating sequence tending to zero) is certainly a necessary condition for a series to converge, but it is generally insufficient — there are evanescent-term series that diverge (e.g., harmonic series).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use more powerful convergence tests (d'Alembert, Cauchy, Abel, etc.) beyond checking that terms tend to zero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternating-series convergence vs absolute convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain alternating series with evanescent terms converge (e.g., Leibnitz-type alternating expansions); however, the series of absolute values may diverge (i.e., conditional convergence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that conditional convergence allows paradoxical rearrangements; absolute convergence guarantees associative and commutative behavior of infinite sums while conditional convergence does not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional convergence allows rearrangement paradoxes; absolute convergence prevents them
rubrics_metrics.description: Dirichlet proved that convergent series of all positive terms permit rearrangement without changing sum. If a series is absolutely convergent (series of absolute values converges), associativity and commutativity hold; if only conditionally convergent, these properties break down and by suitable rearrangement the series can be made to sum to any prescribed number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: freely rearranging terms of a conditionally convergent series; historic examples include paradoxes with the harmonic/alternating harmonic series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple continued fractions always converge; periodic ones correspond to quadratics
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple continued fraction (all numerators 1) always converges. If the continued fraction is periodic it represents a quadratic irrationality; conversely, any quadratic irrationality has a simple periodic continued-fraction expansion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convergents of continued fractions provide rational approximations; the oscillating nature (even/odd subsequences) gives upper and lower bounds and enables error estimation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continued-fraction vs decimal periodicity analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an analogy: periodic decimal series represent rational numbers; periodic simple continued fractions represent quadratic irrationalities. Any real number can be represented either as a decimal expansion or as a continued fraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use continued fractions for good rational approximations to irrationals; periodicity indicates algebraic (quadratic) structure; non-periodicity is consistent with transcendence for certain cases (e.g., π).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rational domain is imperfect (not closed under limits); real domain is perfect (closed)
rubrics_metrics.description: The aggregate of rational numbers is imperfect because there exist convergent rational sequences whose limits are not rational. The aggregate of real numbers is perfect because it contains all its limiting points: any convergent sequence of real numbers represents a real number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: the rational domain does not form a continuum; the real domain (being well-ordered, perfect, dense, unbounded and containing rationals) constitutes the Cantor continuum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties that characterize the real-number continuum
rubrics_metrics.description: The real domain: (1) is orderable (of any two reals a and b we can tell which is greater), (2) has neither first nor last member (unbounded), (3) contains all rationals, and (4) is everywhere dense (between any two reals there are infinitely many reals). Cantor defines a continuum as an aggregate that is both well-ordered and perfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To identify a continuum, verify closure under limits (perfection) in addition to order properties; the intuitive notion of geometric continuity must be reconciled with Cantor's formal continuum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic/transcendental distinction via periodicity and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Periodic continued fractions characterize quadratic irrationalities; limitations on continued-fraction elements (e.g., boundedness) relate to algebraic origin and were used by Liouville to detect non-algebraic numbers. However, infinite processes are in general 'indifferent' to algebra — algebraic methods do not have privileged status in infinite expansions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use structure of expansions (periodicity, growth of elements) to infer algebraic properties; but be cautious: non-periodicity alone does not fully characterize transcendence in higher degrees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of solutions of algebraic/transcendental equations by convergent rational sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: A real solution of an equation (algebraic or transcendental) may be represented by a sequence of rational approximations generated by an algorithm (e.g., root-extraction algorithms); squaring or other operations on the approximations can show convergence of derived sequences to rational limits, justifying identification with the desired real root.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct an algorithm (e.g., iterative root extraction) to produce rational convergents; paraphrase the sequence into an infinite decimal fraction to exhibit convergence and hence representation as a real number.
